text.p: Boris Yeltsin came through seven hours of open heart surgery on Tuesday, but it may be some days before it is clear that the 65-year-old president can recover the full health needed to reassert his authority in the Kremlin.
"The operation was a complete success," said Michael DeBakey the pioneering U.S. surgeon who monitored the treatment.
"President Yeltsin will be able to return to his office and carry out his duties in normal fashion," he told reporters.
Renat Akchurin, who led the surgical team, said: "Now the very important stage of post-operative treatment is starting."

Although the bypass surgery was more extensive than the media had been led to expect, Akchurin said Yeltsin should be well enough in a day or two to take back power from Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Yeltsin had handed over his authority, including Russia's nuclear trigger, to Chernomyrdin, one of several figures who have been jostling for position around the sick president.
Doctors have said Yeltsin may need a couple of months to get fully back to work. Akchurin said it may be nearly a week before doctors could estimate how quickly and fully he would recover.
The president has plenty to do.
He must calm Kremlin squabbles that have raged in his four-month absence and address the economic crisis that sparked widespread strikes and protests on Tuesday over unpaid wages.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, who faces reelection on Tuesday, sent Yeltsin "best wishes for a speedy recovery".
Western leaders see Yeltsin, who led Russia out of communism in 1991, as the best guarantor of Russia's shaky democracy and fear that, without him, Russia would become deeply unstable.

The 50-year-old Akchurin, grey with fatigue after a dawn start and confiding he had tried to forget he was operating on the president, said Yeltsin might not come round before midnight (2100 GMT). Medical staff could then take him off a respirator.
He indicated the president's heart trouble may have been more grave than admitted, saying the number of blockages in his arteries was "much more" than the three or four forecast.
He said the details were Yeltsin's "personal business" and what mattered was that his heart was getting plenty of blood.

Medical experts say the president may face the biggest risks after the surgery. Two German specialists in post-operative complications are on hand. But the sense of relief and congratulation was already palpable among the doctors.

"The operation went better than I expected," said Yevgeny Chazov, the head of Moscow's Cardiology Research Centre where the operation was carried out. Chazov kept increasingly senile Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev alive for a decade in the 1970s.

Yeltsin, who opted for surgery to avoid being consigned to a passive life at the start of a new four-year term, issued a written statement before the operation saying he was confident of recovery and reassuring Russians there was no power vacuum.
"Not for a minute will the country be without a leader with full powers," Yeltsin said. "He (Chernomyrdin) and my other colleagues are tested and reliable people."
Chernomyrdin, 58, and a possible successor, has effectively been running the country since Yeltsin's reelection on July 3.

The president had announced the operation on television in a moment of unprecedented candour on September 5. It ended weeks of equivocation by aides who had explained his absence by saying he had a cold and various other minor ailments.
But the admission that the president, who had two heart attacks last year, needed major surgery also fueled a bitter struggle for influence in the Kremlin.
It involved notably Chernomyrdin, chief of the presidential staff Anatoly Chubais and General Alexander Lebed, a political maverick roped in to the Kremlin to secure victory at the polls.

Yeltsin finally sacked Lebed on October 17 amid a flurry of accusations and counter-accusations of mysterious plots and plans to seize power. Lebed has warned of an army mutiny over unpaid wages, but few analysts see a military bid for power.

The 46-year-old former paratrooper, his popularity assured by his success in ending the deeply unpopular Chechen war, remains a key political figure. Polls show he would be a strong contender for the presidency if Yeltsin had to step down.
If that were to happen Chernomyrdin would rule in the interim with a mandate to hold an election within three months.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, 52, would also be a challenger in a new vote. He complained the Kremlin cheated to beat him in July by concealing that Yeltsin had had a third heart attack days before the second-round vote.
